NSCa and INP. Immediate-early genes JUN, EGR1 and FOS, which are essential for synaptic plasticity, learning, memory, neuronal response to injury, cell proliferation, differentiation, transformation and apoptosis, were upregulated in MDD NSCa and NSCb. Neurogenesis drivers were disrupted at the intermediate stages of the trajectory in MDD, with INP showing lower expression of NELL1, POSTN7 and ADAMT14 metalloproteinases, important for niche functions and cell growth and implicated in neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases14. INP had higher expression of SOX9 (refs. 3,4,36), which favors glial fate by promoting the neuron-to-glia switch and suppressing neurogenesis. Additionally, INP had higher progenitor cell marker ETNPPL3,4, suggesting lagging neurogenesis. Moreover, NBs, which were fewer in MDD, had reduced DCX and trophic factor BDNF, indicating deficient trophism. Catenins, involved in Wnt signaling and cell adhesion, were higher in NSCa and lower in ImGC2, ImGC1 in MDD. Integration of single-nuclei and spatial transcriptomic data of neurogenesis trajectory cell clusters and SGZ niche clusters (sgz.ml and sgz.pl) highlighted concordant upregulated interferon and innate immune response signaling (IFITM3 (ref. 26), MX1 and COL5A3) and blocked cell growth (MT1M37 and APCDD1 (ref. 38)). Niche-associated DEGs included elevated HPCAL1 (ref. 39), involved in calcium binding, neurotransmission and Wnt pathway. Conversely, GC marker CALB1, a mature neuron marker regulating calcium homeostasis, synaptic plasticity and memory, was downregulated in multiple spatial subfields. Few DEGs downregulated in cell and spatial clusters had genome-wide association studies (GWAS) hits for MDD5. These included oncogene SAMD5 (ref. 40), previously found altered in MDD brain tissue, synaptogenesis-linked CSMD3, calcium-dependent cell-adhesion CDH9 (ref. 41), linked to autism and Alzheimer’s disease41 and thyroid-associated TRHDE (Fig. 3j). Moreover, thyroid function-related TTR42, downregulated in NSCb, NB and ImGC2, encodes for transthyretin, which transports thyroid hormones (thyroxine) and vitamin A (retinol) through the bloodstream and cerebrospinal fluid and has mutations that result in transthyretin amyloidosis (a condition where misfolded proteins build up in the heart and nervous system). Transthyretin was reported to be decreased in MDD cerebrospinal fluid and correlating with serotonin turnover and suicidal ideation42.

Reduced neuroplasticity in the hippocampus circuit in MDD To determine the underpinnings of reduced hippocampus circuit plasticity and weakened memory functions in MDD1, we investigated

molecular alterations across all cell and spatial clusters (Fig. 4a–c and Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). The PENK+ GABAergic medium-spiny neuron-like cluster (InN5.PENK) had 566 DEGs, the most compared to the other cell clusters, followed by GC1 with 378, and ExN1.CA1-4. FIBCD1 with 147. Shared dysregulated pathways between MDD neurogenic cells, mature cell clusters and spatial clusters, involved serotonergic pathways, intracellular trafficking, glutamatergic signaling, apolipoproteins, long noncoding RNAs and neuroinflammation (Figs. 3h,i and 4a–c and Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). Supporting serotonergic system involvement in MDD, INPs had lower neurogenesis-associated HTR4 and suicide-associated HTR1E43, ImGC1 had lower HTR7, which promotes neurogenesis, neurite outgrowth and dendritic spine maturation, whereas spatial subfields had lower HTR2A and HTR2C, and InN.PENK had elevated HTR1D. Fourteen solute-carrier family (SLC) genes, suggested as biomarkers of MDD44, were downregulated across NSCb, INP, NB, ImGC1 and ImGC2, and ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1, whereas nine were upregulated in INPs and NBs. RAB6B45, an SLC member, encoding a protein involved with retrograde transport from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum, was upregulated in InN5.PENK, while CLTCL1 (ref. 46), necessary for endocytosis and neurodevelopment, and associated with 22q11.2-linked autism46, was increased in ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1. Meanwhile, DISC1 (ref. 47), coordinating intracellular trafficking and microtubule dynamics, and disrupted in schizophrenia, was downregulated in GC1. Glutamate ionotropic (AMPA and NMDA) and metabotropic receptors were downregulated in MDD NSCa, NSCb, INP, ImGC1, NB and GC1 and in several spatial clusters. Glutamatergic signaling is essential for synaptic plasticity and excitatory–inhibitory balance and has been strongly implicated in MDD48. Among apolipoprotein genes, APOE, involved in lipid homeostasis and neuronal repair, was increased in NSCa and INP but reduced in ImGC2. In various MDD cell and spatial clusters, there were elevated APOL2 and APOD, linked to cellular senescence, and in GC1 there was upregulated APOL6, which induces mitochondria-mediated apoptosis by ferroptosis, whereas ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1 exhibited decreased anti-apoptotic BCL2. Long noncoding RNAs were dysregulated in most cell clusters, including INP, NB, ImGC.1, ImGC.2, InN.PENK, GC1 and ExN1.Ca1-4. FIBCD1. Notably, LINC01515 and LINC02315, both upregulated in MDD, were found to be GWAS hits for autism49, psychiatric disorders (in the Japanese population)50 and suicide (in the Indian population)51.

Consistent with the neurogenic clusters, interferon signaling was upregulated in GC1 and ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1, including ISG15, MX1, CXCL12 (previously implicated in MDD neuroinflammation52) and MAT2B53, involved in blood–brain barrier damage and apoptosis. While immune surveillance by SCART1 (ref. 35) was reduced in neurogenic clusters, InN5.PENK and GC1, together with Sushi Domain Containing anti-inflammatory signaling, and SEMA6D30, which regulates microglia function in Alzheimer’s disease30, was also reduced in NSCb, INP and ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1 (Fig. 4b). Unique to InN5.PENK was overexpression of proenkephalin, a precursor of enkephalins, which modulate pain perception, stress responses and emotional regulation, as well as immediate-early genes ARC, FOS, JUNB, EGRs, and JAG1, upregulated with neuronal activity and cell development. Consistently, neurodevelopment-associated genes were upregulated in InN5.PENK, including NNAT3,4, CAMKV54, microtubule-associated proteins with variants linked to microcephaly, intellectual disability and epilepsy17, CYFIP2 implicated in epileptic encephalopathy55, NPTN linked to autism56 and neurofilament heavy, medium and light chains, which are biomarkers of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and neuronal damage57. Conversely, RELN15, which regulates neuroplasticity and dendritic growth, was downregulated in InN5.PENK. Of note, KRAS58, which is involved in long-term potentiation and hippocampus-dependent learning and memory, was upregulated in GC1 but downregulated in several spatial clusters (Fig. 4b,c), potentially reflecting nuclear versus cytoplasmic expression. HOMER1, a postsynaptic scaffolding protein involved in synaptic plasticity, dendritic structure and bipolar disorder59, had downregulated RNA in ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1 (Fig. 4b). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using DEGs from both single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics highlighted disrupted cellular development, stress and death, signaling and synaptic function, immune response, metabolism, ECM and gene expression regulation in the MDD hippocampus circuit (Methods and Fig. 4d). To characterize gene regulatory networks, high-dimensional weighted gene coexpression network analysis (hdWGCNA) was performed (Fig. 4e–g). The top co-regulated hdWGCNA gene module associated with MDD in GC1 highlighted dysregulated translation, cell migration, axon pathfinding (ROBO) and response to cellular starvation, with central genes in the network regulating ribosome assembly and translation (for example, RPL, RPS, EIF4A2 and EEF1A1), intracellular trafficking and structural plasticity (TUBA4A, TUBB2A and ACTB) and cellular stress (heat shock proteins; Fig. 4e). In ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1, top MDD-associated gene module involved NMDA receptors, dopamine and serotonin release, long-term potentiation, cell–cell junction and communication, and central genes in

the coexpression network were HTR2C and GRM1 receptors, calcium voltage-gated channels (CACNA2D3) and synaptic function genes (Fig. 4f). In InN.5.PENK, top MDD-associated module confirmed altered glutamatergic and GABAergic neurotransmission, synaptic function, long-term potentiation and cell–cell junction, with central genes in the network being GABRB1 and GRIK2 (Fig. 4g).

Proteome changes show altered trafficking, development and neurotransmission in MDD To determine whether transcriptional alterations in MDD are reflected at the protein level, high-resolution shotgun proteomics was performed in bulk anterior hippocampus proper (DG and CA regions; Fig. 5a). This identified 297 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in MDD (Fig. 5b), including downregulated calbindin, which regulates calcium homeostasis, synaptic plasticity and memory, and had downregulated RNA in spatial clusters gcl, sgz.ml, sgz.pl, ca.1, ca.2–4, axons and radiatum (). DEPs functional groups confirmed the same pathways that emerged as altered in MDD when integrating DEGs from cell and spatial clusters (Fig. 5c). Integrating proteome and single-nucleus transcriptome data (Fig. 5d,e), we identified genes dysregulated at the RNA and protein level, including upregulated intracellular trafficking and Golgi-associated RAB6B45, solute-carrier family member SLC25A44, biomarker of treatment response in MDD, CLTCL1 (ref. 46), involved in 22q11.2-associated autism46, NPTN56, linked to calcium homeostasis, synaptic plasticity, neurodevelopment, neurotransmission and autism56, CAMKV54, maintaining dendritic spines54, CYFIP2 (ref. 55), controlling cytoskeletal dynamics and early cortical development, HPCAL1 (ref. 39), regulating calcium signaling, synaptic transmission, and cell differentiation, mitochondria-related PSAP and MDH1, important for oxidative phosphorylation, and MAT2B53, driving neuroinflammation through methylation. Downregulation of ACYP2 (ref. 60) RNA and protein, involved in cellular development and differentiation, links ATP metabolism, telomere length and aging-associated cellular changes to MDD. HOMER1 (ref. 59), with a single nucleotide polymorphism linked to antidepressant response in bipolar disorder, and regulating synaptic plasticity, had lower RNA in NSCa, ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1 and several spatial clusters, whereas the protein was elevated in MDD bulk hippocampus proper tissue (Figs. 4b and 6b,e), suggesting either compensatory downregulation of transcription in response to elevated protein, or cell-type specific downregulation of the RNA, while the protein was elevated across hippocampus subfields and cell types. Transcription factor regulons underly stress-dependent epigenetic changes in MDD To investigate regulatory mechanisms underlying cell-type-specific transcriptional changes, we analyzed single-nucleus chromatin accessibility and TF-binding activity. In MDD, there were 102 differentially accessible chromatin regions (DARs) across cell types, spanning promoters, intronic and distal regulatory regions (Fig. 6a). A subset of MDD DARs overlapped with DEGs, identifying genomic locations where chromatin accessibility directly corresponds to transcriptional changes of nearby genes, suggesting functional regulatory elements. Those DEGs included downregulated SCART1 (ref. 35) (in GC1, ImGC1, ImGC2, InN5.PENK, INP and NB) responsible for immune surveillance and linked to psoriasis35. Regulatory programs were characterized analyzing TF footprinting and binding score driving gene expression. This revealed a central role of zinc fingers, KLF15 and other stress-responsive Krüppel-like factors highly regulated by corticosteroids23 as transcription drivers in GC1, InN5.PENK and ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1 (Fig. 6b). Of note, stress exposure in the last 6 months before death was higher in individuals with MDD than in CTRLs (Extended Data Table 1, Source Data Fig. 1 and Methods). In GC1, the footprinting activity of TF with motif similarity (Fig. 6c) induced higher HPCAL1 (ref. 39) (Wnt and β-catenin), KRAS58 (long-term potentiation), MAT2B53 (methylation and methylation-induced inflammation) and CYFIP2 (ref. 55) (cytoskeletal dynamics and cell development). KLF15 binding correlated with changes in gene expression of HPCAL1 (ref. 39) and KRAS58, and TF occupancy at target loci revealed the association between chromatin accessibility and footprint scores in MDD versus CTRL (Fig. 6d). In InN.5.PENK, footprinting activity of TFs with motif similarity (Fig. 6e) increased expression of CAMKV54 (spine maintenance), RAB6B45 and SLC25A6 (ref. 44) (vesicle trafficking), CYFIP2 (ref. 55) and MDH1 (redox-balance, metabolism), NPTN56 (cell-adhesion and long-term potentiation), while reducing ACYP2 (ref. 60) (maintaining telomeres and protecting against cellular aging). There was a correlation between KLF15 binding and gene expression of CAMKV54, RAB6B45 and SLC25A6 (ref. 44) and TF-binding profiles showed the relationship between chromatin accessibility and footprint scores in MDD versus CTRL (Fig. 6f). In ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1, TFs reduced HOMER1 (ref. 59) RNA, whereas the protein was increased, which is a possible compensatory response

aimed at regulating glutamatergic synapse function, calcium signaling, dendritic spine growth and synaptic stability. KLF15 binding correlated negatively with gene expression of HOMER1 (ref. 59) in MDD versus CTRL, and TF-binding profiles showed a chromatin accessibility signal relationship with footprint scores in MDD versus CTRL, illustrating condition-specific TF occupancy at target loci (Fig. 6f).

Discussion This study provides a multiomic molecular atlas of the adult human hippocampus and its neurogenic niche, identifying dysregulated functional pathways affecting the stem cell progeny and the MDD trisynaptic circuit. Findings support the presence of sustained AHN in adult human brain3,4,36, and the potential for GCs to maintain long-term immature features and undergoing dematuration20. The MDD hippocampus shows altered TF activity affecting chromatin accessibility and expression of genes involved in intracellular trafficking, spines, cell adhesion, telomeres and cellular aging. Conversely, some DEGs were GWAS hits for MDD5, suggesting genetic factors. These were involved in neurodevelopment, synaptogenesis, cell-adhesion and thyroid function, whereas other DEGs had variants linked to neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders. The presence of a neurogenic cell lineage was supported by gene expression and stage-specific TF regulation, replicating recent findings4. Moreover, the existence of a stem cell progeny3,4 was supported by computational trajectory inference strategies both in single-cell and DG niche spatial clusters. Immaturity markers retained in ImGC2, and trajectory inference indicating a path re-entry from GC to ImGC2, suggested extended immature neuronal states3,36, and dematuration potential of human GCs supporting marmoset findings20. The fact that immaturity-associated genes expressed in ImGC2 were found in cell located in the GCL rather than the SGZ, further supports de-differentiation of mature GCs. In MDD, there seemed to be halted AHN, with more quiescent progenitors and fewer neuroblasts. TFs regulated neurogenesis and the trisynaptic circuit in individuals with MDD, who had higher severity of stress exposure in the last 6 months before death compared to CTRL individuals. Notable TFs altered in MDD include the primate-specific progenitor cell marker ETNPPL3,4 and ADAMT14 metalloproteinases, which affect the niche and are disrupted in neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases14. Corticosteroid- and stress-responsive KLF23 footprinting, driving chromatin accessibility together with gene and protein expression, support the previous findings of an association between stress exposure and KLF9 RNA levels in depressed women and female mice, where KLF9 regulated dendritic spines and neuroplastiticy23. Conversely, neurogenic progeny DEGs that were GWAS MDD hits5, suggests that genetic mechanisms affect cell growth (SAMD5 (ref. 40)), adhesion (CDH9 (ref. 41)), synaptogenesis (CSMD3) and thyroid function (TRHDE). Another thyroid-related gene disrupted in the neurogenic trajectory has been linked to suicidal ideation and serotonergic function in MDD (TTR42), supporting a link between thyroid function and mood regulation. As variants of calcium-dependent cell–cell adhesion molecule CDH9 were not only linked to MDD, but also to autism and Alzheimer’s disease41, shared pathogenetic mechanisms between these diseases are possible. This is further supported by the finding that interferon-related genes affecting the neurogenic progeny in MDD have variants associated with intellectual disability (EIF2AK2 (ref. 25), AFF3 (ref. 32) and KCND2 (ref. 33)), Alzheimer’s disease (IFIT3 (ref. 26) and SEMA6D30) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ITM2A31). The other common theme of dysregulation of apolipoproteins and amyloid-related pathways across cell clusters, further supports the hypothesis that MDD is a risk factor for dementia. Additional trans-diagnostic aspects of MDD pathogenesis are shared mechanisms with autoimmune and infectious diseases that can present with neuropsychiatric symptoms, including inflammatory bowel diseases (XKR6)34, psoriasis (SCART1)35, systemic lupus erythematosus (HERC6 (ref. 27) and NRIR28) and COVID-19 (NRIR29). These autoimmune programs were disrupted in the neurogenic cell trajectory, GCs, excitatory neurons and in medium-spiny-neuron-like GABAergic neurons, suggesting a hippocampus-wide effect, which could be the cause or a consequence of the cellular alterations observed in MDD. Previously uncharacterized in the human hippocampus, the medium-spiny-neuron-like GABAergic population was the most dysregulated and had elevated proenkephalin production, and immediate-early genes, suggesting an activated state, possibly underlying the link between MDD, pain, stress response, excitatory–inhibitory balance and emotional regulation. InN.PENK had altered vesicle, spine and adhesion genes, supporting an activated state. At the same time, glutamate48 ionotropic (AMPA and NMDA) and metabotropic receptors were downregulated in the DG neurogenic trajectory and GCs, which could happen in response to cellular stress, as neurogenic cells had elevated immediate-early genes and heat shock proteins, and GCs had increased long-term potentiation (KRAS58) and translational regulation. Therefore, InN.PENK might be attempting to compensate for a stress-hyperactivated DG. Disrupted intracellular trafficking in MDD was shared across cell types and driven by genes already associated with treatment response in MDD (SLC25A44), involved with 22q11.2-linked autism (CLTCL1)46 and with schizophrenia (DISC1)47, whereas tubulins17 and neurofilaments57 have been linked to neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration, suggesting shared pathogenetic pathways in these diseases. Disrupted intracellular transport may affect structural plasticity, (NPTN56, with a variant linked to autism), mitochondria function (CYFIP2 (ref. 55), involved in epileptic encephalopathy), neurotransmission and ultimately memory functions, which are altered in these diseases. The serotonergic system role in neurogenesis and hippocampus neurotransmission in MDD, is supported by lower neurogenesis-associated HTR4 and suicide-associated HTR1E43 in INPs, lower HTR7 in ImGC1, which controls neurogenesis, neurite outgrowth and dendritic spines, lower HTR2A and HTR2C in spatial subfields, and elevated HTR1D in InN.PENK. Additionally, HTR2C was a central hub gene in the ExN1.CA1-4.FIBCD1 gene-regulatory network identified by hdWGCNA. Altered CA excitatory neurons NMDA receptors and HOMER1, a key postsynaptic scaffolding protein regulating synaptic plasticity and glutamatergic communication, supports disruption of neuroplasticity

in this important part of the hippocampal memory circuitry in MDD. Notably, a HOMER1 variant has been associated with lower MRI gray matter volume, higher BOLD functional MRI neural responses to emotional stimuli, lower white matter fractional anisotropy, increased axial diffusivity after lithium treatment, and worse antidepressant response in patients with mood disorders59. Limitations of this study include the cross-sectional nature of postmortem studies, limited ability to separate MDD from suicide pathology because most of the individuals with MDD died by suicide, modest power to investigate adversity-related gene expression changes, and potential effects of cause of death or unrecognized medical illness. This work provides the largest multimodal characterization of the human adult hippocampus, and for the first time identifies MDD-associated changes in cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and gene expression, subfield-specific transcriptomic profiles and the regional proteome, in a deeply phenotyped cohort, avoiding confounders due to pharmacological treatment or drug and alcohol use. These findings provide a molecular framework for understanding the regulation of human adult human hippocampal neurogenesis and reveal disrupted neurogenic programs, which may underlie halted AHN in MDD. In the hippocampus trisynaptic circuit, altered transcriptional regulation, intracellular trafficking, excitatory–inhibitory balance, neuroplasticity, neurotransmission, cellular stress and neuroinflammation may work in concert or represent different pathogenetic mechanisms of MDD subtypes. Shared pathogenetic mechanisms are revealed between MDD and neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative and autoimmune disorders, and some involve genes regulating thyroid function, which are conditions that can all present with neuropsychiatric symptoms. The dysregulation of proenkephalin-producing GABAergic neurons underscores the link between chronic pain, stress, reward and depression. Collectively, these findings establish a brain-based framework for understanding MDD and provide a foundation for precision psychiatry through improved disease phenotyping, biologically informed diagnostic subtyping, biomarker discovery and the identification of new therapeutic targets.

Methods Brain and clinical data collection Brain tissue was obtained with approval from the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) of the New York State Psychiatric Institute, the Human Brain Collection Core of the National Institute of Mental Health, and the Institute of Forensic Medicine, of the Ss. Cyril and Methodius University of Skopje, North Macedonia, and with written informed consent from the participants’ next of kin for brain donation and clinical and sociodemographic data collection. The IRB determined that postmortem brain collection and research does not constitute human subject research as it only involves biological samples from deceased individuals. Brain tissue was rapidly frozen in environmentally safe, nontoxic Freon and stored at −80 °C (ref. 16). Sociodemographic and clinical data collected included age, sex, marital status, education, employment, number of children, childhood and lifetime adversity exposure61, recent (last 6 months) stressful life event severity as per St. Paul–Ramsey scale23, psychiatric diagnosis, comorbidity, length of illness, number of disease episodes, clinical severity as per the Global Assessment Scale, mode of death, and treatment, hospitalization and family histories (Extended Data Table 1 and Source Data Fig. 1).

Study sample Inclusion criteria were negative neuropathological examination; negative traumatic or medical brain pathology; brain pH ≥5.7; sudden death with a short agonal state; negative blood alcohol and brain/blood toxicology for psychotropic medications at death and no psychotropic medication use within 3 months before death except benzodiazepines; no neurological or medical diseases affecting the brain. Individuals with MDD met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders criteria for major depressive disorder without psychosis, bipolar disorder or comorbid substance or alcohol use disorders. Control participants had no psychiatric diagnosis, psychiatric treatment or history of suicide attempts. We included 123 participants; 36.45% of samples from the USA and 63.55% from Europe (Extended Data Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Single-nucleus RNA and ATAC sequencing (snMultiome-seq, 10x Genomics) was performed on hippocampal tissue from 24 CTRL and 12 MDD donors with RNA integrity number (RIN) ≥ 5.7. Following quality control, 74 snMultiome samples (44 CTRL and 30 MDD samples; Supplementary Table 1) from 19 CTRL and 11 MDD donors, with 1–4 technical replicates per donor, were retained for downstream analyses, and Visium v1 and v2 (10x Genomics) were performed on 13 CTRL and 14 MDD donors, each with 1–3 biological replicates (44 samples; Supplementary Table 2). A total of 12 CTRL and 12 MDD samples were used for proteomics, with two biological replicates each. Validation studies included Xenium (four samples), Multiplex RNAscope for PROX1/BHLHE22 + /POSTN (18 samples), Duplex RNAscope for DCX/TUBB3 (22 samples, ACDBio), immunofluorescence for DCX/NeuN (16 samples), immunohistochemistry for nestin (71 samples), Ki67 (42 samples), doublecortin (58 participants), and NeuN (70 samples), and Cresyl Violet staining for Nissl bodies (98 samples).

Tissue processing The flash-frozen right hemisphere hippocampus was used for all studies. Because we showed fewer GCs selectively in the anterior MDD hippocampus61, the anterior hippocampus proper, including the DG and CA regions, was dissected and sections at 2-mm intervals were used for snMultiome-seq (five 50-μm-thick sections), Visium v1 and v2 (two 16-μm sections), proteomics (two 50-μm sections post-fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde), RNAscope (three 14-μm sections) and Xenium (one 10-μm section). According to the Paxinos Atlas62, the anterior hippocampus coordinates range from MNI −13.99 to −32.37, spanning 13.3–30.8 on the inter-commissural line between the anterior and posterior commissures.

For immunohistochemistry validation studies, serial sections at 2-mm interval throughout the whole rostro-caudal axis of the post-fixed (4% paraformaldehyde) hippocampus (4 cm long in humans), comprising the anterior (anterior to the lateral geniculate), mid (spanning along the extent of the lateral geniculate) and posterior (spanning caudally from the end of the lateral geniculate) portions were used. Post-fixation time as 12 h for every 5-mm of tissue block thickness. Nissl staining was performed on sections at 1-mm intervals throughout the region used for each experiment for anatomical orientation, and on sections immunolabeled for nestin and NeuN for glia identification, while DCX-immunolabeled sections were counterstained using nuclear red.

Nuclei isolation and library preparation Tissue (~90 mg) was homogenized with a glass Douce tissue homogenizer (Wheaton, 357542) in 5 ml lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2 6H2O and 0.05% NP-40), incubated on ice (5 min), quenched in nuclear wash buffer (5 ml, 5% BSA, 0.25% glycerol and 0.001% protector RNase inhibitor in PBS), filtered through a 40-μm Corning cell strainer and centrifuged three times at 500g (5 min, 4 °C). The pellet was resuspended in nuclear wash buffer and the final resuspension was ultracentrifuged at 10,000g (30 min, 4 °C) over an iodixanol cushion (Millipore Sigma, cat. no. D1556-250), adapting a published method63. Nuclei isolation using Singulator (S2 Genomics) was performed by processing tissue (~90 mg) and RNase inhibitor (5 μm) with a nuclei isolation bundle (cat. no. 100-288-798), the lysate was filtered and centrifuged at 500g (5 min, 4 °C), and the pellet was resuspended in 2 ml Nuclei Storage Reagent, centrifuged at 500g (5 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in 3 ml Nuclei Debris Removal Reagent for a final centrifugation at 500g (15 min, 4 °C), obtaining similar yield as with manual extraction. Nuclei concentration (2–9 × 106 nuclei per ml) and viability was estimated using Trypan blue and 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) on a Countess II Hemocytometer (Applied Biosystems). Single-nucleus gene expression (GEX) and ATAC libraries were prepared following Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + GEX (CG000338), sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (v4 chemistry, average sequencing depth 83,919 reads/nuclei for GEX and 45,624 for ATAC; Extended Data Fig. 1c–v).

Visium v1 and v2 library preparation We processed 21 tissue sections with Visium v1 and 23 with v2. The v1 sections were mounted on barcoded slides (6.5 × 6.5-mm capture area), v2 sections on Superfrost slides (11 × 11-mm capture area), stored at −80 °C, fixed, stained and imaged following the 10x User Guide CG000160 Rev C for v1 and CG000164 Rev C for v2. The v2 probes were transferred to the slide using CytAssist. The spatial spot diameter was 55 µm with a 100-µm center-to-center distance between spots for both v1 and v2. Visium libraries were prepared following the 10x User Guide CG000239 Rev F for v1 and CG000495 Rev G for v2, sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (v4 chemistry, sequencing depth 66,512 mean reads per spot for v1 and 78,361 for v2,). Data were generated using SpaceRanger v.1.3.0 with spatial 3’ v1 chemistry for v1, and v.3.1.2 with spatial probe-based chemistry for v2. The two technologies were analyzed separately.

Proteomics Shotgun proteomics using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS), was performed on 48 fixed tissue samples dissolved in 0.2% RapiGest SF in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, heated (105 °C for 30 min, then 80 °C for 2 h) and digested with trypsin, run for 120 min, with two chromatograms per biological replicate, using a traveling-wave ion mobility spectrometry MSE mode. Yeast alcohol dehydrogenase (50 fmol) was added as an internal control. Mass spectra

Validation studies For the Xenium 266-probe and 5050-probe assays, frozen tissue was mounted onto a 10.45 × 22.45-mm sampling area, fixed and permeabilized, and probe hybridization, ligation and amplification were carried out as per 10x Genomics protocols (CG000579, CG000581 and CG000582 Rev C). Duplex and Multiplex RNAscope were performed on fresh frozen slide-mounted tissue fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (15 min at room temperature), followed by probe hybridization per ACDBio protocols, including positive and negative control probes. Duplex RNAscope was conducted using a 1:50 ratio of channel 2 (C2, red) DCX probe (cat. no. 489551-C2) to C1 channel (green) TUBB3 probe (cat. no. 601991-C1); the red signal was detected by adding 1:60 Fast Red-B to Fast Red-A, and the green signal was detected by adding 1:50 Fast Green-B to Fast Green-A, slides rinsed and counterstained with 50% hematoxylin (Gil’s Hematoxylin No. 1, Sigma-Aldrich cat. no. GHS132-1L). Multiplex RNAscope was performed following a similar protocol and using probes for POSTN (cat. no. 409181-C1), BHLHE22 (cat. no. 448351-C2), PROX1 (cat. no. 530241-C3) and Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent Kit v2 (cat. no. 323100). Immunohistochemistry was performed by incubating primary antibodies for 5 days with blocking buffer at 4 °C (anti-nestin mouse monoclonal, 1:8,000 dilution, Chemicon cat. no. ST1111-100UL; anti-Ki67 Novocastra mouse monoclonal 1:1 solution Leica Biosystems cat. no. NCL-L-Ki67-MM1; anti-doublecortin guinea pig polyclonal, 1:30,000 dilution, Sigma-Aldrich cat. no. AB2353; anti-NeuN mouse monoclonal, 1:100,000 dilution, Clone A60, Millipore Sigma cat. no. MAB377) followed by incubation with biotin-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted at 1:200, goat anti-guinea pig (Vector cat. no. PI23227) and horse anti-mouse (Vector cat. no. BA-2000), staining using 0.05% 3,3’-diaminobenzidine or nickel-diaminobenzidine (Millipore Sigma) and counterstaining for Nissl substance with Cresyl Violet16,61. For immunofluorescence, antibodies (anti-doublecortin guinea pig, 1:1,000 dilution, Millipore cat. no. AB2253; anti-NeuN rabbit monoclonal, Sigma-Aldrich cat. no. MABN140) were incubated in blocking solution overnight at 4 °C, and with secondary antibodies Alexa Fluor 594 goat anti-guinea pig and Alexa Fluor 488 goat anti-rabbit (1:500 dilution, Jackson ImmunoResearch cat. no. 106-585-003 and 111-545- 003, respectively) and counterstained with DAPI. For both immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence primary antibodies were omitted to exclude unspecific staining16,61. Cell numbers were estimated in the DG region of interest using unbiased stereology software (Stereo Investigator, MBF)16,61.

Single-nucleus multiome data integration and processing GEX count matrices and ATAC fragment files were generated using 10x Cell Ranger v.2.0.0 with Single Cell Multiome ATAC + GEX v1 chemistry. Ambient RNA was removed from GEX matrices using SoupX (autoEst- Cont and adjustCounts, default parameters). Cells were retained if they contained 500–150,000 UMIs, >300 genes and <10% mitochondrial RNA, consistent with published filtering strategies for high-sensitivity 10x datasets63 and rare neurogenic cell populations3. Low-quality cells (<300 genes and >10% mitochondrial RNA; Supplementary Fig. 1a) and doublets identified using scDblFinder were removed. ATAC peak BED files were converted to GenomicRanges objects and merged into a unified peak set. Peaks on nonstandard chromosomes, within hg38 blacklist regions, or >10 kb or <20 bp were removed. Cells with transcription start site enrichment <1, nucleosome signal >3 or 200–100,000 ATAC reads were excluded (Supplementary Fig. 1a). All 74 samples were merged in both modalities. Cells that passed quality control were retained for further analysis.

GEX data were processed with Seurat. After normalization (NormalizeData), the top 2,000 highly variable genes were identified (FindVariableFeatures) and, together with 93 curated neurogenesis-associated genes, scaled using ScaleData. Principal-component analysis (PCA) (RunPCA) was performed, and the top 40 principal components (PCs) were batch-corrected with Harmony (RunHarmony) using sample, donor and batch as covariates (Supplementary Fig. 1b–e). ATAC data were processed with BPCells and Signac. BPCells enabled disk-backed storage of the peak matrix. Peaks were TF-IDF normalized, reduced by latent semantic indexing (LSI), and batch-corrected with Harmony using LSI components 2–40 and donor, sample and batch as covariates (Supplementary Fig. 1f,g). WNN analysis was performed with FindMultiModalNeighbors using the top 30 Harmony-corrected PCs and LSI embeddings (prune. SNN = 1/20). The resulting graphs were used for UMAP and Leiden clustering (FindClusters, algorithm = 4, resolution = 0.8). Differential gene expression across the 31 clusters was assessed by pseudobulk linear mixed-effects modeling with SpatialLIBD, including sample, batch, sex, scaled age and winsorized RIN and post-mortem interval (PMI, time from demise to brain collection, measured in hours) as fixed effects and donor as a random effect. Clusters were annotated using canonical gene expression per human hippocampus snRNA-seq studies3,4,36,65,66 (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 2a). Data were integrated with published snRNA-seq datasets3,36,65,66 (Extended Data Table 2) using reciprocal PCA integration. External datasets were preprocessed with Seurat67 and Harmony, and cluster correspondence was assessed by Pearson correlation of average expression across the top 5,000 variable genes (Extended Data Fig. 3a–m).

Multiome neurogenic cell trajectory identification Because one astrocyte cluster (Astro2) and one GC cluster (GC2) expressed immaturity-associated genes3,36,65,66, we hypothesized that GC and astrocyte populations contained neurogenic cells. We therefore subset these clusters and repeated the Seurat workflow (normalization, dimensionality reduction, Harmony integration, WNN analysis and clustering), identifying 17 unsupervised clusters. Among the 17 clusters obtained, we selected cells enriched with known early, intermediate and late neurogenesis markers3,4,36, and then applied FindSubClusters at 0.5 resolution. We annotated cell clusters based on their enrichment with canonical neurodevelopmental and neurogenesis-associated markers and, for visualization purposes, the remaining mature GC and astrocyte clusters were merged together as mGC and mAstro, whereas GC4 was maintained separately as it expressed immune and GC markers, suggesting microglia engulfment (Fig. 2a,b). Cells were annotated as NSCa when expressing neuronal-lineage-associated ASCL1 with SOX2 (ref. 16), RMST, a long noncoding RNA regulating neurogenesis by interacting with SOX2 (ref. 16), PAX6 (ref. 68) and LAMA2 (ref. 69), encoding an ECM protein that maintains NSC niches, promotes progenitor survival and dictates the transition from stem cells, and RSPO2, essential for neurogenesis. Cell defined as NSCb expressed NES16, FABP5 and FABP7, regulators of NSC proliferation and survival, ID3 (ref. 70), which inhibits early differentiation, SFRP2, a modulator of the Wnt signaling pathway and TPPP3, encoding a microtubule-associated protein that regulates microtubule dynamics, bundling, and cell mitosis. Cells were annotated as INPs when enriched with neurogenic STMN1 and STMN2 (ref. 18), TUBB3 (ref. 17), NNAT3,4 and NEUROD6. NBs were identified by expression of classic neurogenic marker DCX16, with ST8SIA2 (ref. 16), which drives polysialylation, CALB2 (refs. 3,4), RELN15 and NELL1 found in neuroblasts and neuroblastoma cells. Two clusters expressing PROX1 were annotated as immature GCs: ImGC1, expressing INSM1, encoding for zinc-finger TF involved in embryonic neurogenesis, and NEUROD1 (refs. 3,4), necessary for neuronal differentiation, whereas ImGC2 expressed developmental genes BHLHE22 (ref. 6), FST9, OTOF71, POSTN7 and SMAD7 (ref. 24).

Clusters were validated by applying gene signature scoring with ScoreSignatures_UCell using canonical markers for NSCs, INPs, NBs and ImGCs3,4,18 as features (Fig. 2c). To compare transcriptional profiles of the putative adult neurogenic trajectory with embryonic neurogenic cells, we integrated NSCa, NSCb, INP, NB, ImGC1 and ImGC2 data with a fetal hippocampus snRNA-seq dataset68 (in Seurat using reciprocal principal component analysis (PCA) with SCTransform (SCT) normalization and 3,000 integration features), including fetal PROX1+ GCs, AQP4+ astrocytes and three types of ASCL1+ progenitors, while OPCs were excluded (Extended Data Fig. 4b–d).

Neurogenic cell trajectory inference Neurogenic trajectories were inferred with Monocle72 and Palantir73, using NSCa as the root population. Pseudotime, terminal state probabilities and entropy were computed, and gene expression was denoised with MAGIC. Gene expression dynamics and modules were analyzed, and the neurogenic subtrajectory was isolated for downstream analyses. For visualization and analysis, neurogenic populations were randomly downsampled to 10,000 cells each. Trajectory-dependent differential gene expression was assessed with Monocle3 using the model pseudotime × diagnosis.

Transcription factor binding analysis on cell trajectory clusters TF regulation along the neurogenic trajectory was analyzed using TOBIAS74 and pySCENIC (Fig. 2h). Neurogenic ATAC peaks were called with Signac75 CallPeaks from MACS3, corrected for Tn5 bias, footprinted and analyzed with BINDetect to infer TF-binding dynamics using JASPAR76 motifs, excluding ENCODE blacklist regions. Peaks were annotated with UROPA, and TF activity visualized using motif binding z-scores. Gene regulatory networks were inferred from GEX data with PySCENIC72 (GRNBoost2; Fig. 2i), pruned, and repeated 50 times to retain robust regulons (>20% of runs; Fig. 2i). AUCell scores were calculated for each cluster, and regulon activity was compared to TF-binding dynamics to identify stage-specific regulatory programs.

Spatial gene expression data processing, integration and cluster annotation Visium v1 and v2 data were loaded into Seurat (Load10X_Spatial), normalized, variable features identified and data scaled using standard Seurat workflows. Replicates were merged and PCA, UMAP, neighbor graph construction and clustering were performed using the top 30 PCs; spots with fewer than 500 UMIs were excluded from downstream analyses. Unsupervised spatial clusters were identified with Seurat (FindClusters, resolution of 0.34) and annotated by marker gene expression and hippocampal anatomy. Low-abundance clusters were removed, yielding 13 clusters in Visium v1 and 17 in Visium v2 (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3), each represented across all samples. Shared clusters included the granule cell layer, SGZ (with molecular and polymorphic layers), choroid plexus, inhibitory neurons, axons, dendrites and vasculature. Visium v1 contained a combined stratum lucidum/radiatum cluster, whereas v2 resolved these into separate lucidum and radiatum clusters and identified a distinct CA2 cluster. Differential gene enrichment analysis was performed on each cluster by pseudobulked linear mixed-effects modeling, including sample, batch, sex, scaled age and winsorized RIN and PMI as fixed effects, and donor as a random effect, implementing the SpatialLIBD package77.

Integration of single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic data To determine how snMultiome-seq cell clusters anatomically map onto hippocampus subfields, anchor-based integration using snMultiome-seq as reference and Visium v1 and v2 and Xenium as

query datasets was performed by FindTransferAnchors and Transfer- Data in Seurat67, assigning spatial spots probability scores based on transcriptional congruence (Fig. 1g–j).

Neurogenic niche spatial trajectory inference by RNA velocity on Visium data To probe the existence of a trajectory in the DG neurogenic niche, gene expression dynamics across hippocampus spatial clusters were analyzed, focusing on sgz.pl, sgz.ml and gcl, which expressed proliferation, differentiation, maturation and neurogenesis markers among their top 100 (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). RNA velocity was computed on Visium v1 (55 × 55μm spots, poly(A)-based) using velocyto78 and scVelo following BAM sorting with SAMtools. Velocity was estimated using the dynamical model after PCA on the top 5,000 variable genes plus 55 neurogenesis-associated genes and construction of a 30-nearest-neighbor graph, PAGA was used to infer connectivity and branching between spatial spots, and latent time to estimate where each spots lay between the beginning and end of a trajectory (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h).

Statistical analyses comparing participant and biospecimens characteristics Pairwise comparisons were performed using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for age, PMI, brain pH, RIN and snMultiome RNA/ ATAC quality metrics and chi-squared tests were used to compare sex distribution between MDD (n = 55) and CTRL (n = 68) participants (Extended Data Fig. 1c–l). Resulting P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure and an FDR-adjusted P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Linear regression analyses were performed within diagnostic groups to assess relationships between RIN and age, PMI and brain pH in the full cohort with available RIN values (n = 76 participants), and in cohort selected for the omics studies (n = 38 participants and 74 samples; after removing 3 samples after quality control; Extended Data Fig. 1m–v and Supplementary Table 1) with a P value < 0.05 considered as statistically significant.

Analysis of differential gene expression and accessible chromatin in MDD versus CTRL Differential gene expression and chromatin accessibility between MDD and CTRL were analyzed on cluster-level pseudobulk data using limma. Count and peak matrices were aggregated by biological sample and cluster without merging samples from the same donor processed in different batches. Pseudobulks with fewer than five cells or spots were excluded. Models included cell/spot number, winsorized RIN and PMI, age, sex, sample and batch as fixed effects, with within-donor correlation estimated using duplicateCorrelation. Lowly expressed genes were filtered with filterByExpr (edgeR), normalized using TMM (calcNormFactors), and analyzed with voomWithQualityWeights, lmFit and eBayes to account for variable sample quality and repeated donor measurements. For NSCs, INPs and NBs, DEG significance was defined as P < 0.05 log2FC > 1 to reduce type II error due to low cell numbers (Fig. 3h); for visualization only, these findings were shown in a single volcano plot. For ImGC1, ImGC2 (Fig. 3i), all other snMultiome clusters (Fig. 4a), and all Visium v1/v2 clusters (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b), DEGs were defined as FDR < 0.05 and log2FC ≥ 0.5.

Differential protein expression analysis between MDD and CTRL Proteomic data were analyzed with the Rosetta Elucidator Protein Expression Analysis System, and peptide identifications were assigned with Mascot against the UniProt/SwissProt human canonical protein database with isoforms. DEPs were defined as those with >2 peptides and P < 0.05. Duplicate protein accessions were collapsed before Reactome pathway enrichment using ReactomePA and

clusterProfiler (Benjamini–Hochberg correction; minGSSize = 10, maxGSSize = 500), and related pathways were grouped into parent categories (Fig. 5a,b).

Differential transcription factor binding analysis in MDD versus CTRL Following differential chromatin accessibility analysis, TF-binding activity between MDD and CTRL was inferred across all snMultiome cell clusters using TOBIAS74 (Fig. 6b). Cluster-specific peaks were called with MACS375 via Signac75, corrected for Tn5 bias (ATACorrect), footprinted (ScoreBigWig), and analyzed with BINDetect to identify differential TF binding between MDD and CTRL (Fig. 6d,f,h). ENCODE blacklist regions were excluded, peaks were annotated with UROPA, and vertebrate TF motifs were obtained from JASPAR76. BINDetect results were filtered to TF motifs with differential binding (P ≤ 0.01) and only predicted target DEGs retained in the corresponding cluster and overlapped with DEPs (Fig. 6c,e,g). These TF–target pairs were used to construct regulatory networks linking TF binding, gene expression and protein expression, with edge weights representing log2 differential binding scores and gene nodes colored by DEG logFC (Fig. 6c,e,g). KLF15 binding profiles at target loci were visualized using PyBigWig and Matplotlib (Fig. 6d,f,h).

Cell abundance estimation in MDD versus CTRL Differences in neurogenic cell proportions between MDD and CTRL were tested using β-binomial generalized linear mixed models (glmmTMB) in each neurogenic cluster using the same covariates as for the differential gene expression and accessible chromatin analyses (Fig. 3c). Duplex RNAscope, immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence data were compared between MDD and controls using Welch’s t-test in Prism (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). For Multiplex RNAscope, linear models in R (using the same covariates as for the differential gene expression and accessible chromatin analyses) tested the effect of MDD on the abundance of GCL and SGZ cells coexpressing PROX1 with POSTN or BHLHE22, or all three markers (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h).

High-dimensional weighted gene coexpression network analysis The hdWGCNA79 was performed in Seurat67 on all unsupervised clusters (Fig. 4e–g). After normalization, scaling and Harmony batch correction, metacells were generated within each cluster-sample group (≥100 cells; 20 Harmony dimensions, k = 25). Signed coexpression networks were constructed, gene modules were identified and module eigengene connectivity (kME) was calculated. Reactome pathway enrichment was assessed using Enrichr via the hdWGCNA pipeline. Module–diagnosis associations were tested with linear mixed-effects models, including diagnosis as a fixed effect, sample and batch as random effects, and age, PMI and RIN as covariates, with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction.

Pre-ranked gene set enrichment analysis Pre-ranked GSEA was performed with clusterProfiler using genes ranked by logFC × −log10 (Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P value). Differentially regulated KEGG and Reactome pathways were identified (minGSSize = 10, maxGSSize = 400, P < 0.05, including Benjamini– Hochberg FDR correction) and related pathways were collapsed into parent categories.

Analysis of trans-diagnostical involvement of MDD dysregulated genes and proteins Neuropsychiatric disease enrichment was assessed using psygenet2r (PsyGeNET80; database = ‘ALL’). Cell cluster significant DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d) and DEPs (Fig. 6f,g) were analyzed with psygenetGene to identify associated psychiatric disorders.

Highlights

•  A spatial atlas of the human hippocampus was created based proteomic, transcriptomic, and

epigenomic analyses of neurotypical humans and subjects with major depressive disorder.

•  An experimental and computational framework for understanding cellular identity, neighborhood,

RNA dynamics, and gene regulatory states with spatial contexts.

• Spatial epigenomic analyses demonstrate that CREB5 and FOS play key roles in neuronal excitability.

## Abstract

We present the first spatial tri-omic (proteomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic) taxonomy of human

hippocampus, addressing two key challenges in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics: visualizing cell

morphology and epigenetic gene regulation in situ. By designing and multiplex imaging a novel panel of

25 protein targets, we generated the first large scale spatial proteomics map of the hippocampus at single

cell resolution (330 nanometers). Through integrated spatial proteomic and transcriptomic analyses, we

identified canonical hippocampal subfields and distinct cell types within the dentate gyrus and cornu

Ammonis (CA). RNA synthesis rates were the highest in the CA pyramidal neurons than any other

hippocampal subfields. To map gene regulation, we applied state-of-art spatial ATAC-seq to identify open

chromatin regions and cis-regulatory elements, revealing how chromatin landscapes differ across

hippocampal subfields. These regional differences help explain why certain neurons are more excitable

and recruited for circuit formation, as their chromatin is open and responsive to transcription factors.

Together, these approaches created the most comprehensive spatial atlas of the human hippocampus

to date, consisting of over 1.6 million single cells from 16 individuals. This study demonstrates the use of

spatial proteomics and epigenomics to investigate the molecular neuropathology of human brain in both

healthy and diseased states.

Keywords: spatial omics, spatial epigenomics, spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, human

hippocampus

## Introduction

The human hippocampus is essential for memory formation and spatial navigation and is critical in

the limbic–cortical–striatal–pallidal–thalamic circuits that regulate mood, emotions, and learning. The

hippocampus contains structurally distinct subfields, including the dentate gyrus (DG) and cornu

Ammonis (CA) regions CA1, CA2, and CA3 1, and shows significant cellular and molecular diversity 2. A

comprehensive understanding of the hippocampus's cellular and molecular landscape is crucial for

studying normal brain functions and the mechanisms underlying various neurological disorders.

The cellular taxonomy of the human brain has primarily been investigated through two methodologies:

single-cell analysis and spatial transcriptomics. Previous single-cell studies have provided a cell type-

specific RNA database of the human hippocampus 3-7, but these data lack spatial context due to the

dissociation involved in single-cell extraction from postmortem brain tissues. Dissociation disrupts cell-

cell contacts and cell integrity, leading to the loss of neuronal and glial processes. Single-nucleus RNA

(snRNA) sequencing from isolated nuclei also fails to capture transcriptomic information from the cytosol

and neuropil, which constitute the majority of neuronal volume and are vital for synaptic activity. These

components are crucial in the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders 8,9. Lack of spatial information

mean that cellular subtypes and function cannot be mapped to their original microenvironments. For

example, within the hippocampus's trisynaptic circuit, granule neurons in the DG project to pyramidal

neurons in CA3, which then relay signals to pyramidal neurons in CA1. The perforant path from the

entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus to the DG, and projections from CA1 to the subiculum and

fornix, are integral to this circuit 10. The precise connections are critical, but current understanding is

hampered by the dearth of spatial data.

Recent spatial studies based on cytoplasmic mRNA capture indicate that there is considerably cellular

diversity in the human prefrontal cortex 11 and mouse brain 12-14. Further, layer-specific gene profiles have

shown that dysregulation of gene expression is associated with schizophrenia and autism spectrum

disorders 11. Previous studies have not, however, fully elucidated the complexity of human hippocampus

morphology, function, and epigenetic molecular characteristics 15,16.


<!-- Page 7 -->


4

In this study, we present the first spatial multi-omic atlas of the adult human hippocampus based on

proteomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic profiling. We evaluated 17 hippocampi from 9 neurotypical

donors and 8 donors with major depressive disorder (MDD) (Figure 1A) (Table 1). The subjects had a

mean age of 44 ± 12 years, with 15 males and 2 females. RNA quality consistently high across all

hippocampal samples, with a mean RIN of 7.58 ± 0.88. The hippocampus is essential for understanding

MDD due to its pivotal role in the brain's mood and cognition circuits 17,18. Abnormally small hippocampal

volumes 19,20 and altered neuronal connectivity 21 are linked to MDD, especially in untreated adolescents.

These structural changes as well as aberrant interactions between the hippocampal DG and emotion-

regulation areas like the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex are indicative of disruptions in critical neural

pathways in patients 22. Additionally, chronic stress, common in severe MDD, leads to reductions in apical

dendrites of hippocampal pyramidal neurons and disrupted synaptic connections in rodents 23.

We established a new experimental and computational workflow in spatial proteomics for

neuroscience, which includes a custom-designed panel of 25 protein imaging targets to generate high-

resolution cellular maps that included 1.6 million cells in human hippocampus. Importantly, this spatial

proteomics approach preserves the tissue morphology and original cell organization, ensuring precise

mapping of protein localization within the natural context of the tissue architecture. This dataset enables

downstream bioinformatic study of cell-cell distance, microenvironment, protein-protein relationship, and

protein-mRNA correlation. Spatial proteomic data offered unprecedented resolution of cellular

morphology at the single cell level, with a larger detection area of tissues than spatial transcriptomics.

Integration with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics allowed us to quantify the relative abundances of

each cell type in hippocampal subfields and revealed variable RNA levels in MDD hippocampi compared

to healthy control samples. RNA velocity analysis showed high inter-subject heterogeneity particularly in

CA pyramidal neurons that was not observed in controls, suggesting that cell-type and gene-specific

transcriptomic instability are characteristic of MDD. Genome-wide chromatin accessibility data at 50 µm

resolution were obtained using our state-of-art spatial-ATAC-seq technology 24. For the first time, the

epigenome of the human hippocampus was profiled with spatial contexts. Hippocampal subfield-specific


<!-- Page 8 -->


5

transcription factors were identified based on open chromatin read peaks and motif sequence. Spatial

ATAC-seq revealed the epigenetic regulation of different cell types in the hippocampus and showed that

the chromatin states in granule neurons are more readily accessible for cFOS binding, indicating a primed

state for memory formation. Together, we introduce and exemplify the use of spatial proteomics and

spatial epigenomics in neuroscience research. This work provides a multi-omic atlas of human

hippocampus for the research community. Our study highlights the importance of preserving spatial

context in neurological research and underscores the potential of using spatial multi-omics to bridge the

gap between traditional single-cell analyses and a more comprehensive, integrated understandings of

brain function and disease.

## Results

Single-cell taxonomy of human hippocampus by spatial proteomics

The primary aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize the neuronal, glial, immune, and

stromal compartments within the architectural landscape of the human hippocampus using proteomic,

transcriptomic, and epigenetic techniques (Figure 1C). To minimize confounding factors, we specifically

selected postmortem human brain samples from cases of sudden death, ensuring the availability of

comprehensive medical records and clear toxicology profiles. Medical, psychiatric, and psychosocial

histories of all subjects (including controls) were determined through chart reviews and psychological

autopsy 25, with appropriate written informed consent obtained.

We first performed 25-plex Co-Detection by Indexing (CODEX) 26 of hippocampal tissue from nine

neurotypical controls and seven MDD patients (Figure 1D, Table 1). The 10-µm thick brain tissue sections

were stained with a panel of 24 antibodies and 1 cell nuclei marker, sequentially imaged, processed, and

systematically quantified (Figure 2A-C) employing methodologies previously reported 27. Distinct cell

types, including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia, were identified and visualized

based on spatial coordinates (Figure 2D-E). The utilization of postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD95)

and Neurofilament-L (NFL) markers facilitated the demarcation of major dendrite-enriched and axon-


<!-- Page 9 -->


6

enriched regions, respectively (Figure 2C). Following the quantification of protein marker expression, we

used unsupervised clustering to identify six major cell types: neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes,

microglia, vascular cells, and immune cells in the CTRL01 neurotypical hippocampus sample (Figure 2F).

In one slice of the CTRL01 sample, a total of 82,009 cells were identified and analyzed systematically

(Table S1). Cell type-specific markers, such as NeuN and BDNF for neurons and OLIG2 for

oligodendrocytes, were used to annotate the clusters (Figure 2G).

We observed variable expression percentages of the apolipoprotein APOE among different glial cell

types. While previous studies suggested APOE+ cells are primarily astrocytes and,

occasionally, microglia 28, we found APOE expression in astrocytes (35.96%), microglia

(13.30%), oligodendrocytes (23.79%), and vascular cells (18.04%) (Figure 2H). The percentage of

APOE+ oligodendrocytes was slightly lower than their total population percentage (28.54%).

We next overlaid the distribution of cell types onto their original spatial coordinates to characterize

the hippocampal neuroanatomy structures (Figure 2I). The DG stratum granulosum was distinguished by

the exclusive presence of small and densely packed granule neurons (Figure 2F, 2I). The DG stratum

moleculare was enriched in dendrites (PSD95+) and separated from the CA by the vestigial hippocampal

sulcus. The DG polymorphic layer united the granular layer to CA4 and was enriched in axons

(Neurofilament-L+) of granular neurons. From the ventricular cavity toward the vestigial hippocampal

sulcus, key layers of the CA were identified including the stratum pyramidale, molecular zone, and

stratum oriens (Figure 2F, I). The DG stratum granulosum has mostly neurons, whereas the CA molecular

zone is composed mostly of oligodendrocytes (Figure 2J). The rest of the regions have a heterogenous

mixture of different cell types. The DG stratum granulosum has the highest neuron-to-glia ratio (14.95) of

all hippocampal regions (Figure 2K). The diverse compositions of cell types suggest that the

hippocampus consists of spatially heterogeneous subfields with organized pathways important for neural

processing and synaptic connectivity.

Multi-cellular neighborhoods and cell-cell distance


<!-- Page 10 -->


7

When we expanded our analyses to all samples, nine neurotypical control samples and seven MDD

samples, we identified eight cell types (Figure 3A). Crucially, no significant batch effects were observed

(Figure 3B). In addition to the six cell types identified from CTRL01, we identified choroid plexus epithelial

cells and leptomeningeal cells when evaluating all samples. The choroid plexus epithelial cells were

exclusive to CTRL04 (8.96%) and CTRL05 (4.61%), whereas leptomeningeal cells were identified in

MDD01 (2.73%), MDD04 (5.11%), MDD07 (2.92%), CTRL02 (3.48%), CTRL04 (0.75%), CTRL05

(0.44%), CTRL07 (5.35%), and CTRL08 (0.33%) (Figure 3C and Table S1). The observed distribution of

cell types aligned with the canonical anatomical regions of the brain (Figure 3D), validating our spatially

resolved proteomic approach.

To investigate the spatial organization of these cell types, we examined cellular neighborhoods

(CNs) of the hippocampus by identifying similar cell-type enrichment patterns using a nearest neighbor-

based approaches.29 We identified nine distinct cellular neighborhoods (Figure 3E-F). Two CNs stand

out as particularly enriched with vascular, immune, and choroid plexus epithelial cells: CN0 (Astrocyte

Immune) and CN4 (ChPx_Epi Immune). Potential differential functionality likely arises due to the

presence of astrocytes in CN4 but not in CN0. CN2 (DG Neuron) is enriched for granule neurons and

has a pattern consistent with the DG stratum granulosum (Figure 3F). CN3 (CA Neuron) is enriched for

both neurons and astrocytes, mirroring the patterns observed in the CA. Collectively, these findings

highlight the power of CODEX imaging and neighborhood analysis to identify conserved brain regions

that both consistent the gross anatomical knowledge and also discover finer molecular regional

nuisances, pinpointing functionally distinct microenvironments within the intricate landscape of the brain.

In subjects with MDD, enduring priming of microglia has been reported (Rahimian et al., 2022; Wang

et al., 2022). In our study, we observed that the distances between microglia and neurons, as well as

between microglia themselves, were closer in MDD hippocampi than in control hippocampi (Figure 3G).

This observation suggests that microglia may migrate toward neurons in MDD brains, contributing to

neuronal inflammation. Understanding the specific contributions of these interactions in the context of


<!-- Page 11 -->


8

MDD could shed light on the intricate interplay between the immune system and the neurobiology of

depression.

Spatial transcriptomic heterogeneity in the human hippocampus subfields

Spatial proteomics defines the cell types and phenotypes at single cell level, whereas spatial

transcriptomics provides an unbiased molecular readout to identify the gene programs and pathways

underlying those phenotypes. Integrating the two modalities enables discovery of mechanisms that

cannot be inferred from a predefined protein panel alone. We used the DBiT-seq technology 30 to profile

mRNAs in the hippocampi of staged flash-frozen postmortem human brains from six neurotypical controls

and six MDD patients (Table 1, Figure 1A-C, Figure S1). Each hippocampal tissue section, with the DG

positioned in the center, measured approximately 1 x 1 cm² and was 10 µm in thickness. These sections

were spatially barcoded (50 x 50 µm2 in pixel size, 2500 spots in 5 x 5 mm2 sequencing area), followed

by cDNA synthesis and sequencing library generation as previously described 31 (Figure 1B). To confirm

that the accuracy of regional annotation was free from effects of technical factors, we performed spatial

mRNA-seq on biological replicates of three brains.

The resulting transcriptomic atlas revealed regional cellular heterogeneity in the subfields of the DG

and CA (Figure 4A-D, Figure S2A-C). Based on a control brain (CTRL04), we examined gene expression

in each cluster and annotated each cluster with its regional location. In total, unsupervised clustering of

mRNA profiles identified seven hippocampal sub-regions (37,500 pixels in total): 1) GCL; 2) pyramidal

neuron region of CA; 3) hilus region that contained inhibitory neurons; 4) molecular layer, polymorphic

layer, and hilus; 5) white matter; 6) vasculature, immune cells, and other cells; and 7) choroid plexus

(Figure S2D). Using genes highly expressed in each cluster, the signaling pathways active in each

subfield were assessed (Figure 4E-F). NEUROD2 and GRIN2A were expressed in all neurons, whereas

PROX1 was expressed by granule neurons and SCN3B was highly expressed in pyramidal neurons of

the CA (Figure 4G-I, Figure S2A). SST was expressed in one subtype of inhibitory neurons (Figure 4J).

Astrocytes expressing NDRG2 and AQP4 were enriched in the molecular layer of the DG and white

matter, but not in the DG granule cell layer (GCL) (Figure 4K-L). Oligodendrocytes, which were identified


<!-- Page 12 -->


9

by expression of MOBP, which encodes a myelin sheath protein, were located in the white matter (Figure

4M). Microglia were sparsely detected in all regions (Figure S2B). Epithelial cells, which express high

levels of CLDN5, were abundant in the choroid plexus (Figure 4N). The cell-type assignments were

confirmed by neuropathology analyses of adjacent Nissl-stained sections. Additionally, we compared the

spatial proteome data and spatial transcriptome data of the samples. RBFOX3 mRNA and the NeuN

protein that it encodes were both detected in all neurons (Figure 4O-P). PSD95, predominantly located

in the dendrites of excitatory synapses, marked the dendrite-enriched polymorphic layer, molecular layer,

and hilus (Figure 4Q). The distribution of AQP4 highlighted the astrocyte-enriched region (Figure 4R);

this region was also marked by expression of NDRG2 and AQP4 mRNAs (Figure 4K-L).

Cell type deconvolution by integration with reference single-nuclei RNA datasets

Comprehensive mapping of the abundance of distinct cell types with high sensitivity and accuracy in

human hippocampus region is challenging because cell types and densities vary substantially in

subfields. Unsupervised clustering of spatial transcriptomes and snRNA-seq data mapped the pixels

corresponding to the major cell types but did not allow determination of the cell-type compositions of each

pixel (Figure 1B, S3A-C). The machine learning computational pipeline cell2location accounts for latent

variables in techniques, batches, and varying cell density across locations 13. Using cell2location, we first

derived the reference gene signatures from a previously reported snRNA-seq dataset (n= 219,058 nuclei,

69 cell subtypes) 3 and then computed the relative cell-type abundances in our spatial spots. The resulting

maps were consistent with anatomical hippocampus subfields (Figure 4T-U, S3E-F). For instance,

granule cells were most abundant in the DG GCL as predicted. Similarly, pyramidal neurons mapped

onto the CA3 region (Figure 4U, S3F-G). Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes were preferentially distributed

in the white matter and DG molecular zone. We detected five subtypes of inhibitory neurons (InN SST

ADAMTS12, InN NR2F2 ANO2, InN NR2F2 SLC17A8, InN LAMP5 NMBR, InN LAMP5 CHST9)

previously described in hippocampus 3,32. These showed diverse distribution patterns in our study (Figure

S3D, S4). As expected, vascular and leptomeningeal cells were detected in choroid plexus, and pericytes


<!-- Page 13 -->


10

were found close to vasculature (Figure 4T-U). We validated cell-type annotations in all representative

regions by neuropathological review on adjacent Nissl-stained sections following published morphology

criteria 33 (Figure 4A).

We performed non-negative matrix factorization of cell-abundance estimates from cell2location to

detect co-localized cell types, although it should be noted that signature marker genes greatly

overlapped. Nineteen distinct cellular compartments with varying cell compositions were detected (Figure

S3D). Four types of oligodendrocytes (Oligo CPXM2 KANK4, Oligo OPALIN SLC5A11, Oligo OPALIN

LAMA2, Oligo OPALIN LINC01098) co-localized (Figure S3D). In contrast, inhibitory neuron subtypes

(InN SST ADAMTS12, InN LAMP5 CHST9, InN NR2F2 SLC17A8, InN NR2F2 ANO2) did not co-localize

(Figure S4). Inhibitory neuron subtypes spread out in a mutually exclusive distribution pattern, whereas

oligodendrocyte subtypes shared a niche. We mapped the most abundant cell types in each pixel in a

representative MDD sample (Figure S3E-F) and observed a consistent pattern of each cell type

distribution in the hippocampus subfields. The fine-grained cell maps of 12 human hippocampi (Figure

S3G) could be used as a resource for understanding the co-occurring cell type combinations in brain

function and disease.

RNA velocity analyses reveal region-specific cell states involved in synapse plasticity

To understand the kinetics of cell states in the human hippocampus, we computed RNA velocities

based on the sequencing counts of nascent pre-mRNAs and mature (i.e., spliced) mRNAs, using the

state-of-the-art method scVelo 34,35. RNA velocity, the time derivative of the gene expression state, was

computed based on differential equations that model the kinetics of transcription, splicing, and

degradation of mRNA molecules. The balance between unspliced and spliced mRNAs is predictive of

cellular states, where high levels of pre-mRNA indicate high levels of gene expression, and an excess of

spliced mRNA indicates low levels gene expression. The velocity profiles of each gene in each single cell

reveal information about RNA turnover with high accuracy and throughput.


<!-- Page 14 -->


11

Spatially variable patterns in RNA expression (Figure 5A-F) and RNA velocity (Figure 5G-L) were

observed for genes involved in neurotransmitter transport and synapse plasticity regulation. For instance,

the glutamate transporter SLC1A2 was expressed at high levels and its RNA velocity score was high in

the DG stratum moleculare region (Figure 5A, G). This represents a pattern of high expression with rapid

turnover. The mRNAs encoding two GABA transporters, SLC6A1 and SLC6A7, had complementary

mRNA expression distributions: SLC6A1 was expressed at high levels in the white matter region, but

SLC6A7 was predominantly detected in the neuron-enriched CA region (Figure 5B-C). Regions with high

mRNA levels of SLC6A7 displayed a low turnover of RNA synthesis (Figure 5C, 5I). This represents

another correlation pattern of high expression with slow turnover. Furthermore, there were considerable

regional differences in genes associated with synaptic vesicle trafficking and cytoskeleton remodeling

such as CLSTN2, PCLO, and TTLL7 (Figure 5D-F, J-L). This spatial atlas of RNA velocity will provide a

valuable resource for identifying molecules that change with age or disease, which could potentially be

quantified using magnetic resonance imaging or positron emission tomography.

those with MDD. In other words, cell states, not cell types, are altered in MDD.

Next, we investigated how the cell states differed in hippocampal subfields from a perspective of RNA

addition to group effects, the region of the pixel significantly influenced RNA dynamics. After adjusting

for age, PMI, and within-sample correlation, the differences in the proportion of mature mRNA between

in the WM. The increased variation in the MDD group may reflect clinical heterogeneity among subjects,

such as differences in disease severity, stress exposure, benzodiazepine treatment, and brain changes

in agonal stage.

We observed three types of transcriptomic stages, induction, repression, and steady state, by

examining the velocity and expression of the most dynamic genes. Excess of pre-mRNA relative to the

computed equilibrium rate indicated an induction stage. BCAS1, a gene encoding a myelin sheath protein

in oligodendrocytes, was at the induction stage in white matter (Figure S5D). In spatial anatomical spots

with high expression of BCAS1, this gene also had a high RNA velocity score (Figure S5D). MAP1B, a

gene encoding a protein involved in neuron microtubule assembly, was detected in all three

transcriptomic stages in a manner that depended on the spatial location. In most GCL and CA spots the

RNA velocity score of MAP1B was close to zero, indicative of an mRNA in equilibrium, but some white

matter and hilus spots had positive RNA velocity scores indicative of induction stage and others had

negative RNA velocity scores indicative of repression (Figure S5E). The velocity and expression of

MAP1B were highly heterogeneous in the sub-regions of hippocampus, suggesting some areas are

undergoing dendrite outgrowth 36, while others are not.

Interestingly, certain genes, such as GRIN2A and NRGN, exhibited opposing trends in velocity and

expression in specific regions (Figure S5F-G). NMDA receptors are involved in long-term synaptic

potentiation, a key process in memory and learning 37. GRIN2A, which encodes a subunit of the N-methyl-

D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, showed high expression but low velocity in most granule cell layer (GCL)

and CA regions (Figure S5G), suggesting an equilibrium state. In certain spots within the hilus and

molecular layer, GRIN2A displayed positive velocity, indicative of induction. The differential spatial

pattern of GRIN2A suggests distinct RNA states, leading us to hypothesize that GRIN2A may function

differently depending on its spatial localization. One possible explanation is that the granule cells in

dentate gyrus (GCL) requires a steady state of GRIN2A to support long-term potentiation, whereas the

hilus may trigger a transient increase in GRIN2A expression only during spontaneous excitatory

neurotransmission. This finding highlights the strength of spatial transcriptomics in dissecting cell states

and their functional roles.
