Spatially resolved chromatin accessibility profiling identifies region-specific epigenetic

alterations in the MDD hippocampus

We detected region-specific alterations in gene expression and RNA dynamics within the hippocampi

of individuals with MDD compared to neurotypical controls. To understand the underlying gene regulatory


<!-- Page 18 -->


15

mechanisms, we utilized spatial-ATAC-seq 24 to profile chromatin accessibility in 13 biological samples

collected from five control and five MDD subjects (Fig. 6E, Table 1). A spatial barcoding scheme was

applied to tag accessible genomic loci with Tn5 transposition, thus achieving cell-level resolution,

genome-wide mapping of chromatin accessibility in the tissue samples.

We calculated transcription factor motif scores to identify the key regulators of gene expression as

described previously 40. The motif scores serve as a quantitative measure of the likelihood of binding of

a transcription factor at each pixel. By comparing the spatial plots for mRNA, RNA velocity, and

transcription factor motif scores, we identified several spatial patterns. CREB5, a member of the

CREB/ATF family, is involved in diverse physiological processes including memory formation, synaptic

plasticity, and long-term potentiation 41. CREB5 RNA expression and RNA velocity scores were highly

correlated in the fimbria (region annotated in Figure 4A) and glia cell-enriched CA region, but the

transcription factor motif scores were high in the pyramidal neuron-enriched CA region and low in the

fimbria (Figure 6A). This suggests that pyramidal neurons in CA were more excitable via CREB5-induced

gene expression than were granule neurons in GCL, because the former cells were primed with open

chromatin at CREB5 motifs.

Spatial ATAC-seq offered a way to visualize the differential excitability of neurons, detecting patterns

that are not apparent in mRNA expression level. FOS, a transcription factor involved in synaptic plasticity

42, exhibited no distinct spatial pattern in mRNA expression (Figure 6B). Although FOS gene expression

levels were low - consistent with the sparse numbers of FOS-expressing cells involved in memory

formation 43, the high motif scores suggest that most granule neurons in GCL are competent to rapidly

activate cFOS-driven transcription, facilitating the recruitment of neuronal ensembles for new memory

encoding.

NFIA, a member of the nuclear factor I transcription factor family, regulates astrocyte activity, which

is necessary for memory formation and neuronal transmission 44. This gene was highly expressed in the

GCL region and moderately throughout the other regions of the tissue (Figure 6C). RNA velocity scores


<!-- Page 19 -->


16

were lower in the GCL region, as were transcription factor motif scores, than in other areas of the

hippocampus.

NFE2L1, a nuclear factor, is essential for neuronal health and maintenance 45. NFE2L1 mRNA

expression was high in the CA but low in the GCL and white matter areas (Figure 6D). In contrast, RNA

velocity was low throughout the entire tissue. The NFE2L1 motif score was also very low across the

tissue. It was previously reported that some post-synaptic neurons are more excitable than their

neighbors 46. Our approach offers an epigenetic explanation for this phenomenon: region-specific

chromatin accessibility primes the cells to respond to different memory formation processes.

To understand the downstream transcription factor activity in MDD, we imputed the single-pixel gene

expression levels using gene scores as previously described 47. A positive correlation between gene

scores and motif scores indicates activator function, while a negative correlation suggests repressor

activity. Multiple activating and repressing transcription factors were identified (Figure 6E). For example,

ETV6, which regulates the maintenance of the developing vascular network in the brain 48, was identified

as an activator and FOXG1 was identified as a repressor.

To further resolve region-specific patterns of accessibility within the hippocampus, we performed

unsupervised clustering of the thirteen spatial-ATAC-seq samples. The GCL cluster (highlighted in circle,

*Figure 6F) was distinct and aligned with the anatomical GCL region identified by Nissl stain on an*

adjacent tissue section (Figure S6A-C). The other clusters were localized throughout the CA region,

where inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia were distributed at varying

proportions (Figure SF6D-G). In MDD, transcription factors enriched in the GCL

included MEF, FOXG1, RAR, ZNF, and IRX family members, while depleted transcription factors

included several SOX and NFI family members (Figure 6G).

To examine the impact of genetic variants on the chromatin accessibility in MDD, we sought to identify

chromatin peaks located close to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with MDD, based

on a genome-wide association meta-analysis 49. There were variations in chromatin accessibility between

MDD and controls within genes known to be mutated in subjects with MDD that are related to


<!-- Page 20 -->


17

neurotransmitter transport (e.g., SLC6A7), synaptic plasticity (e.g. CAMK2A), and ion transport (e.g.

CACNA2D1) (Figure 6H). Notably, the polymorphism rs2240795 is located within the coding region of

SLC6A7 and most likely alters chromatin structure in this locus. The differential peaks in CACNA2D1

presumably resulted from nearby polymorphisms rs37078 and rs10265730. CAMK2A, which encodes a

epigenetic alterations in the GCL of MDD samples relative to controls and identified differentially

regulated transcription factors and gene modules that are potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

## Discussion

We report here a comprehensive atlas of the human hippocampus generated using spatial multi-

omics technologies. We demonstrated the best technological practices and interpretable findings of

spatial proteomics, spatial transcriptomics and spatial epigenomics. Fresh frozen human brains stored

for up to 18 years proved to be a reliable source of RNA and DNA for spatial assays. Our atlas provides

functional insights about cell types and cell states in health and disease, revealing region-specific

signatures in cellular and molecular landscapes in controls and MDD subjects. For the first time, the

morphology and cell-cell interaction information were detected in the human hippocampus at single-cell

level by spatial proteomics, comprising over 1.6 million cells. In addition to cell types, we also profiled the

cell states by RNA dynamics in each hippocampal sub-field. Highly dynamic genes were identified,

including CLSTN2 and SST, that displayed a different RNA velocity in MDD than CTRL. Specifically, the

pyramidal neurons in CA3 had higher RNA turnover in MDD versus control subjects. We demonstrated

that RNA velocity is a predictor in cell state progression. An altered balance of pre-mRNAs and mature

RNAs was observed more often, and the ratio was more variable in the MDD than control brains. The


<!-- Page 21 -->


18

identified dynamic genes may serve as labeling targets for future in vivo neuroimaging or

pharmacokinetics studies.

Previous studies suggested that early life stress impacts DNA methylation in the hippocampus and

implicated epigenetic gene regulation induced by childhood adversity in MDD 50,51. Our spatial-ATAC-seq

results identified the CREB family transcription factors as critical regulators of transcription in the CA and

FOS/JUN family as most important in the DG. We compared the chromatin accessibility between MDD

and control hippocampal samples and located the open chromatin regions that may regulate genes

previously associated with MDD 49. Interestingly, spatial-ATAC-seq can be used to infer whether a

transcription factor is an activator or a repressor, depending on the correlation of motif scores and gene

scores. Our approach offers a method to study epigenetic regulation in tissue samples with high spatial

precision. The analysis of motif scores provides a novel perspective on neuronal allocation and

excitability in memory formation. We utilized spatial-ATAC-seq to visualize and predict regions where

memory formation is likely to occur. Future work investigating other immediate early genes is expected

to delineate the molecular mechanisms underlying how distinct neurons are recruited to a memory

engram. Additionally, our integrated mRNA and epigenetic analyses have the potential to delineate the

spatial organization of “cellular memory”, revealing, for example, whether repeated exposure to

environmental stressors produces disproportional glial responses in psychiatric disease.

In conclusion, we have described our pioneering characterization of human hippocampal proteome,

transcriptome and epigenome. We demonstrated that RNA velocity and chromatin accessibility data

provide novel perspectives on the differences between healthy and MDD brains. The spatial omics

resources generated in this study will serve as valuable references for researchers studying neurological

diseases and for comparative studies between the human brain and brains of other organisms.

Limitations of the Study

While our spatial multi-omic dataset provides significant insights into the cellular and transcriptional

diversity of the human hippocampus, we did not incorporate spatial data registration with MRI images or


<!-- Page 22 -->


19

investigate the anterior-posterior anatomical axis of the hippocampus. Unlike mice, where hippocampal

structure is more uniform, the human hippocampus exhibits unique cellular organization. Much like

fingerprints, no two human hippocampal sections align perfectly. Even within the same human brain, the

left and right hippocampi may differ. Future studies will require high resolution MRI scans of the brain

prior to spatial profiling to accurately register tissue sections to their anatomical planes.

Previous single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) studies have demonstrated cell-type-specific

gene expression differences between the posterior hippocampus—crucial for cognitive functions—and

the anterior hippocampus, which is involved in mood regulation 5. Due to natural variations in sectioning

orientation, obtaining identical coronal planes across different individuals is not feasible. In our study, we

primarily used coronal sections taken around the mid-region of the hippocampus. This variability

emphasizes the need for representative sampling along the entire anterior-posterior axis to construct a

comprehensive functional atlas of the hippocampus.

We did not investigate the effects of brain lateralization. The dominance of brain hemispheres adds

another layer of complexity; memory processing and other cognitive functions can differ between the left

and right hippocampi. Unfortunately, our study lacked information regarding the brain dominance of the

sampled individuals, which may influence hippocampal function and gene expression.

Although spatial proteomics provides single-cell resolution at approximately 300 nm, current spatial

mRNA-seq and ATAC-seq technologies lack this level of resolution. Future advancements in spatial

technologies will necessitate new designs for higher pixel resolution and larger mapping areas to

enhance detection capabilities. Integrating data across different omic platforms will further improve the

accuracy and depth of spatial profiles.

Current spatial biology findings lack depth and confidence in functional interpretation, due to limitation

of the cohort size. Human samples inherently vary in demographics, processing, and biological

heterogeneity. For instance, MDD is a complex disorder characterized by diverse clinical symptoms and

heritability. Generalization of any spatial findings will require a much larger sample size. Data such as

disease severity, age of onset, family history, stress exposure, body mass index, education level, and


<!-- Page 23 -->


20

history of childhood adversity should also be collected and incorporated into future analyses. Additionally,

we did not investigate the impacts of antidepressant treatment, cause of death, or postmortem interval

on the transcriptomic changes in the brain. Systematic analysis of these factors, enabled by larger spatial

and single-cell multi-omic datasets, will provide greater confidence and clarity in understanding their

functional roles. Future studies incorporating larger cohorts will be essential for addressing these

limitations.

Experimental models and subject details

Postmortem human specimens

This study used de-identified human postmortem brain tissue from the Brain Collection of New York State

Psychiatric Institute (NYSPI) (samples CTRL01, CTRL03 - 09, MDD01 - 08) and the National Institute of

Mental Health's Human Brain Collection Core (sample CTRL02) (Table 1). The NYSPI receives brain

donations from North Macedonia, approved by the local Institutional Review Board. Autopsies were

performed at the Institute for Forensic Medicine and Criminology at Ss. Cyril and Methodius University in

Macedonia. Neuropsychiatric diagnoses, toxicology reports, and medical records were collected and

preserved as previously described 52. In this study, the cohort included nine brains from subjects with no

DSM-V psychiatric diagnosis and eight from subjects with MDD. Subjects were selected based on the

following criteria: 1) sudden death with a short post mortem interval less than 48 hours; 2) no infectious

disease (e.g., HIV, hepatitis, or untreated tuberculosis) or pre-existing neurological conditions; 3) no

coma for 12 hours or more before death; and 4) high RNA integrity of the brain cortex tissue with RIN >

7.0. Neuropathological and toxicology examinations were performed after brain tissues were collected.

Donor’s blood, urine, and hair were collected for toxicology tests. 192 of the most commonly prescribed

or abused substances in Macedonia were tested by state-of-the-art liquid chromatography/quadrupole

mass spectroscopy at the Biomarkers Laboratory Resources (Core Lab) at the Irving Institute for Clinical


<!-- Page 25 -->


22

and Translational Research, Columbia University. Chart review and psychological autopsy 25 were

performed to determine medical, psychiatric, and psychosocial history of each subject (including controls)

with written informed consent from legally authorized representatives.

Brain tissue handling and preparation

We prepared flash frozen unfixed slices of the anterior-mid hippocampal region on the glass slides for

spatial multi-omics assays. Briefly, coronal sections of the right brain hemisphere were serially cut at 20-

mm intervals, held in shape with metal plates, and frozen in Freon. Tissue blocks were selected as close

to the mid DG as possible (Figure 1A-B). We defined the anterior hippocampus (HPC) as the region from

the rostral end of the hippocampus to the start of the lateral geniculate, and the mid HPC as the section

from the lateral geniculate's onset to its disappearance. The rest of HPC region was defined as posterior

HPC. A coronal section of DG regions (~1 cm x 1 cm), identified by the same neuropathologist, were

sliced at 10 µm and placed onto the center of the ultra-clean glass slide (Electron Microscopy Sciences,

63478-AS). All samples were stored at -80 °C before use.

RNA quality analyses

RIN number was assessed at the Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center at Columbia University.

The RIN of brain cortex was determined and used to pre-screen the samples for inclusion. The RIN of

hippocampus (Table 1) was determined on slices adjacent to the slice used for sequencing. Two fresh

frozen tissue slices were placed in a 2-mL centrifuge tube, and RNA lysis buffer (Qiagen, #79216) and

one 5-mm stainless steel bead (Qiagen, #69989) were added. The tissue was disrupted at 25 Hz for 4

minutes with a Qiagen TissueLyser II. Total RNA was isolated following the manufacturer’s instruction

using miRNeasy Micro Kit (Qiagen, #1071023). RIN number was calculated based on the RNA

electrophoresis using a Bioanalyzer (Agilent 2100) or a TapeStation System (Agilent 4200).

Immunohistology and imaging


<!-- Page 26 -->


23

Prior to conducting the spatial proteome profiling experiment using CODEX, we validated each primary

antibody in human hippocampal tissue. Fresh frozen brain slices (10 µm) on glass slides were thawed at

room temperature for 15-30 minutes before staining. Slices were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at room

temperature for 15 minutes, followed by three washes with Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline

(DPBS). We used the peroxidase immunohistochemistry kit (Fisher, PI36000) following manufacturer’s

instructions. Samples were first blocked with the peroxidase suppressor to quench endogenous

peroxidase activity and then with 5% BSA solution with 0.05% Triton-X-100 for 2 hours at room

Cellular neighborhood analysis

In this study, we conducted a neighborhood analysis following a previously described method 58. Firstly,

we utilized a window size of 40 nearest neighbors across the tissue cell-type maps. Within each window,

we quantified the cells of each type, generating vectors representing cell counts. Subsequently, these

vectors were subjected to clustering to identify commonly composed neighborhoods. After an extensive

parameter search, we identified nine cellular neighborhoods that provided the most unique insights into

the spatial organization and heterogeneity of cell types within the tissue. We used heatmap to visualize

what cell types are uniquely enriched in each neighborhood.

Spatial context maps

Spatial context maps were created to understand the hierarchical relationship among neighborhoods as

previously reported 59. We used window size of 45 nearest neighbors for each cell for creation of the

composition vectors. Subsequently, we determined the combination that included the fewest

neighborhoods that made up more than 85% of the neighborhoods within that window instead of

clustering the vectors of neighbor compositions. This combination informs about prominent associations

of neighborhoods in the window, a feature termed spatial context. We counted each combination and

connected the most prevalent combinations together into a spatial context map.

Integration of spatial proteomes with snRNA-seq using MaxFuse

We performed MaxFuse to integrate our CODEX data with snRNA-seq data reported by Franjic et al. 3

as previously described 60. In brief, MaxFuse is a computational algorithm that matches cells across

different modalities through fuzzy smoothing, canonical correlation co-embedding, iterative smoothing,

and matching. Both shared and unshared features are utilized by MaxFuse to boost the accuracy of

matched cells across RNA (thousands of features) to protein (<30 features). Joint embedding with all

features preserves the cumulative information across many genes. We initiated MaxFuse with all gene

features in snRNA-seq and CODEX data to construct a nearest-neighbor graph for each modality

separately. Through meta cell construction (meta-cell size = 2), the sparsity in snRNA-seq data was

dampened. MaxFuse smoothed the weakly linked features between snRNA-seq and CODEX data and

then calculated a shared co-space to embed both modalities. For initial matching using shared features

(<30), we assigned equal weights of 0.3 to both modalities. The matching process was iteratively refined

by learning information from all features in both modalities. Cross-modal cell pairs were filtered using a

threshold of 0.5 to obtain refined cell pairs of high quality. Subsequently, these refined cell pairs were

employed to propagate the matching to the remaining cells. Poor matches between snRNA and CODEX


<!-- Page 31 -->


28

cells were eliminated using a cutoff prediction score of less than 0.3. In our CODEX data, over 98% of

cells were successfully matched to those in the snRNA-seq dataset.

DBiT-seq microfluidic device fabrication and assembly

The microfluidic device was fabricated with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) using soft lithography using the

design previously described 30,31. The chrome photomask with 50-µm channel width were obtained from

Front Range Photomasks. Master wafers for microwells were fabricated using SU-8 negative photoresist

(Microchem, SU-8 2050) as follows: SU-8 was spin-coated on a clean silicon wafer at ~3000 rpm for 40

seconds to yield feature heights of 50 µm. We followed manufacturer’s (MicroChem) recommendations

to perform SU-8 photo lithography, development, and baking. PDMS microfluidic chips were then

fabricated via a replication molding process. The PDMS precursor was prepared by combining Sylgard

184 PDMS part A and part B (Dow Corning) at a 10:1 ratio. After stirring to mix, the mixture was poured

into the master wafer, degassed for 30 minutes (or longer if there were bubbles), and cured at 75 ˚C for

at least 2 hours. The solidified PDMS slab was cut out, peeled off, and the inlet and outlet holes were

punched with a toggle press (Schmidt) to complete the fabrication. The inlet holes were 2 mm in diameter

and held up to 10 µL of solution (depending on the PDMS height). A pair of microfluidic chips with the

same location of inlets and outlets but orthogonal microfluidic channels in the center were fabricated as

a complete set of devices for flow barcoding a tissue slide. For this, the PDMS slab was attached to the

tissue section glass slides and a custom-designed acrylic clamp was used to firmly hold the PDMS

against the tissue specimen to prevent leakage between microfluidic channels.

Region annotations in the hippocampus

The Seurat package (v4.0.4) in R (v4.1.0) was used to assign region identities to each pixel in the

unsupervised clustering results. First, normalization and variance stabilization of transcriptome data for

each pixel with regularized negative binomial regression was performed using “SCTransform”, a module

in Seurat. The process was similar to that widely used for scRNA-seq data normalization, with each pixel

treated as a single cell. The expression matrix of all pixels was SCTransformed (“NormalizeData”,

“ScaleData”, and “FindVariableFeatures”). Unsupervised clustering of spatial data identified distinct

clusters, representing different cell layers in the hippocampus. We assigned a region identity to each

cluster based on gene expression in spatial maps. For instance, a cluster with high levels of PROX1 and

SEMA5A was identified as GCL. To validate our annotations, two neuropathologists reviewed the

adjacent slides with Nissl staining and identified cell types by their nuclei and cytoplasm morphologies

following known criteria 33.

Differentially expressed genes between samples or cell types were identified by using the FindMarkers

function in Seurat. The following parameters were used: min.pct = 0.05, logfc.threshold = log(2). The top

genes in each comparison group (CTRL_GCL vs. MDD_GCL; CTRL_CA vs. MDD_CA; CTRL_WM vs.

mRNA results and screened over 10,000 SNPs previously found in a genome-wide meta-analysis for

MDD 49. Gene scores were calculated using a decay function by summing the signal centered around

the gene promoter 64. To identify regulators, we computed accessibility scores for known transcription

factor-binding motifs at the single-cell level using chromVAR 40. We then calculated the variation between

MDD and controls by the transcription factor motif scores.

GSE214144 (Reviewer token: slirmaoqzpuffkt). We did not generate codes for novel algorithms. Custom

codes were available upon request without restrictions.
